title: Parallel lines and the covariant derivative
one_line_summary: Builds a derivative of vectors that works in curved spacetime: parallelism is defined from the viewpoint of observers trapped in a surface, the naive derivative of v = v^mu e_mu is split into component change plus basis-vector change, the basis change is packaged into connection coefficients Gamma (shown to be non-tensorial and non-zero even in flat polar coordinates), the covariant derivative nabla_u v and its along-a-curve form Dv/dlambda are defined, parallel transport becomes nabla_u v = 0, and metric compatibility nabla g = 0 is argued from length preservation, pointing ahead to Gamma built from dg.
role_in_book: Second chapter of Part II. Chapter 6 argued that gravity is geometry and that spacetime is locally flat; before any equation of motion or curvature tensor can be written, the book needs a way to compare and differentiate vectors at different points. This chapter supplies that tool in a light, component-first way (connection coefficients, covariant derivative, parallel transport, affine parameters, four-velocity along curves, metric compatibility), so that Chapter 8 can write free fall as a geodesic, Chapter 9 can extract Gamma efficiently from the metric (eqn 7.37 is quoted in advance) and Chapter 11 can build a genuine curvature test from Gammas and their derivatives (as margin note 7 promises). Rigour is explicitly postponed: the transformation law of Gamma, covariant derivatives of general tensors and the Leibniz rule are promised for Part V (Chapter 34 revisits the covariant derivative in pictures), in keeping with the book's spiral design.

assumed_background.topic: Vectors expanded on basis vectors, v = v^mu e_mu, with the summation convention and up/down index placement
Plane polar coordinates and position-dependent basis vectors e_r and e_theta
Why the position (displacement) vector cannot be used in general coordinates
Parametrized paths through spacetime and proper time
Tensor classification (m,n) and the tensor transformation law with Jacobian factors
Metric tensor as g(e_mu, e_nu), dot products and lengths of vectors
Local flatness and the Minkowski metric as the small-region limit
Partial derivatives, chain rule, Leibniz product rule, limit definition of a derivative
Gradient and directional derivative of a scalar field in Euclidean 3-space
Intuition for a sphere embedded in 3D space: great circles and tangent planes

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why a vector drawn as a straight arrow between two points is useless on a curved surface and why tangent vectors to curves are used instead.
Reader can state what it means for observers confined to a surface to call two vectors at different points parallel, and why such vectors look rotated to an observer using the embedding space.
Reader can differentiate v = v^mu e_mu with the product rule and identify the extra term coming from position-dependent basis vectors.
Reader can define connection coefficients through de_mu/dx^alpha = Gamma^lambda_{alpha mu} e_lambda and compute them by brute force for plane polar coordinates.
Reader can argue from the polar-coordinate example that non-zero connection coefficients do not by themselves signal curvature.
Reader can explain, using the inhomogeneous second-derivative term in the transformation law, why Gamma is not a tensor.
Reader can write the component formula v^mu_{;alpha} = v^mu_{,alpha} + Gamma^mu_{alpha lambda} v^lambda and use comma/semicolon notation fluently.
Reader can form the directional covariant derivative nabla_u v = u^alpha nabla_alpha v and state the parallel-transport condition nabla_u v = 0 in components.
Reader can parametrize simple curves, recognise when a reparametrization is affine, and write the tangent vector u = (dx^mu/dlambda) e_mu.
Reader can describe Dv/dlambda as 'transport the later vector back, subtract, divide, take the limit' and check that it reduces to dA^alpha/dlambda in flat Cartesian coordinates.
Reader can state metric compatibility nabla g = 0 and show, via the product rule, that it is what keeps lengths of parallel-transported vectors fixed.
Reader can write covariant derivatives of (0,2) and (2,0) tensors, with the sign pattern for lower and upper indices, and use them to check g_{mu nu;alpha} = 0.

teaching_approach.summary: A short, deliberately non-rigorous chapter that moves from a picture to a recipe. It opens with ants and humans confined to a curved surface to motivate an insider's notion of parallelism, then turns immediately to components: the product rule applied to v^mu e_mu exposes a basis-change term, which is named, computed by brute force for flat polar coordinates, and flagged as non-tensorial. Word equations in large brackets ('change in vector' minus 'change due to coordinates') carry the conceptual load before and after each formula. The authors then generalize from basis directions to arbitrary directions by analogy with the Euclidean directional derivative, recast everything along parametrized curves (introducing D/dlambda, the tangent vector and the four-velocity), give a limit-based picture of the derivative using parallel transport back to the starting point, and finish by asserting that the metric forces this connection through the compatibility condition, proved heuristically from length conservation. Almost all heavy lifting (transformation law of Gamma, tensor covariant derivatives, Leibniz rule, Gamma from the metric) is quoted and deferred to Chapter 9 or Part V.
narrative_arc: Motivating need: physics is written as fields and their derivatives, and ordinary derivatives of vectors break in curved spacetime (chapter opening).
Model of a curved spacetime: a manifold covered by many small flat maps, like street maps patched over the globe, locally Minkowskian (Example 7.1).

Insider viewpoint: observers trapped in a surface cannot use chord-like arrows, so vectors are tangents to paths; parallelism is defined by carrying local axes along and keeping components unchanged (§7.1, Figs 7.1-7.3).

Conceptual split: the change of a vector along a direction equals its intrinsic change plus a contribution from the changing coordinate system; the covariant derivative keeps only the intrinsic part (eqn 7.1).
Warm-up from calculus: gradient and directional derivative in Euclidean space as the template for a derivative along a vector (Example 7.3).
Formalism: product rule on v^mu e_mu, definition of connection coefficients from derivatives of basis vectors (eqns 7.5-7.6).
Check by brute force: flat plane in polar coordinates has non-zero Gammas, so Gamma is not a curvature detector (Example 7.4); symmetry of Gamma noted (7.9).
Caveat: Gamma is not a tensor because of the second-derivative term in its transformation law (Example 7.5).
Assemble the covariant derivative nabla_alpha v and its semicolon components; flat Cartesian check gives ordinary derivatives (eqns 7.12-7.19, Example 7.6).
Generalize to arbitrary directions via the connection operator, analogous to u . grad f (eqns 7.20-7.23).
Parallel transport becomes the equation nabla_u v = 0, read as component change equals coordinate-induced change (eqns 7.24-7.27).
Move to curves: parametrization, affine reparametrizations, vector fields, D/dlambda along a curve, tangent vector and four-velocity with u.u = -1 (§7.4).
Picture of the definition: transport the vector at lambda_0 + epsilon back, subtract, divide and take the limit (Example 7.9, Fig. 7.6); flat-space check with the chain rule (Example 7.10).
Closing constraint: the metric fixes the connection through nabla g = 0, justified by requiring lengths to survive parallel transport (§7.5, Example 7.11).
Forward look: since g_{mu nu} = e_mu . e_nu and Gamma comes from derivatives of e_mu, Gamma should be built from first derivatives of g (boxed rule 7.38; formula 7.37 quoted for Chapter 9).
signature_moves: Large-bracket word equations (eqns 7.1, 7.4, 7.27, 7.28, 7.30) state each derivative in plain language before or alongside its components.

Frames curved space from the standpoint of confined observers (ants on a football, people on the Earth) who are forbidden to use the embedding space, and contrasts their judgment of parallelism with that of an outside observer (Figs 7.1, 7.2).
Uses a flat space in curvilinear coordinates (plane polar) as the 'brute force and ignorance' test case, extracting a separation between coordinate effects and genuine curvature.
Relegates notation bridges to margin notes (nabla_alpha = nabla_{e_alpha}; components of derivative versus derivative of components; comma/semicolon shaded box) so the main line stays short.
Gives an operational four-step recipe for the covariant derivative (take later vector, transport back, subtract, divide and limit) paired with a labelled diagram (Fig. 7.6).
Checks each new formula against flat spacetime in Cartesian coordinates, where it must collapse to ordinary partial or total derivatives (Examples 7.6, 7.10).
Uses boxed-symbol arrow rules (dg -> Gamma) as a dependency map of which geometric objects are built from which; the text says this link will be expanded in coming chapters.
Quotes results that will be derived later (transformation law of Gamma, tensor covariant derivatives, Gamma from metric) with explicit forward pointers rather than deriving them now.

sections.title: Chapter opening: why a new derivative, and manifolds as patched maps
sections.summary: States the goal: equations for fields in spacetime need derivatives of vectors and tensors, and curvature undermines the usual rules. Example 7.1 introduces a manifold via the analogy of covering the curved Earth with many small rectangular street maps that join smoothly; spacetime is likewise covered by locally flat four-coordinate charts, looks Minkowskian over small enough regions, and can be curved on larger scales. A margin note pictures a 2D manifold as a smooth, unpunctured rubber sheet.
key_moves: Physics needs differential equations for fields, hence a derivative of vectors valid in curved spacetime
Earth's surface: flat street maps work only locally but can be stitched smoothly over the globe
Spacetime as a smooth manifold covered by local four-coordinate maps
Smoothness implies Minkowski-like behaviour over sufficiently small regions; curvature shows up over larger distances

sections.title: Parallelism
sections.summary: Observers are confined to a curved 2D surface and may not use the surrounding 3D space. A vector as a directed chord between points leaves the surface (New York to Paris tunnel), so vectors are instead tangents to paths. On a path that does not turn according to the insiders, such as a great circle, the tangent is judged the same everywhere; moving a vector so that it matches the local tangent is parallel transport. Generalizing, insiders carry their local axes along and call vectors parallel when they have equal components in these carried frames; from outside, those same vectors appear to rotate (Fig. 7.1; London and Tokyo north directions). Example 7.2 contrasts vectors that are parallel in R^3 but not tangent to a sphere (Fig. 7.2) with correctly transported vectors on the sphere (Fig. 7.3). It closes by setting a requirement for what follows: differentiating a field made of mutually parallel vectors has to give zero.
key_moves: Forbid use of the embedding space: all measurements are made within the surface
Replace chord vectors by tangent vectors to paths
Tangent of a non-turning path (great circle) is declared parallel to itself along the path
Parallelism for general vectors: equal components in local frames that are themselves transported
Outside view: insider-parallel vectors appear to change direction (Fig. 7.1)
Embedding-parallel vectors fail to be tangent to the sphere, so they are not parallel for insiders (Example 7.2, Fig. 7.2)
Requirement carried forward: the derivative of a parallel field must be zero

sections.title: Derivatives and connections
sections.summary: Separates the change of a vector into its intrinsic change and the change caused by position-dependent coordinates, defining the covariant derivative in words as the former (eqn 7.1) and noting that it is directional. Example 7.3 recalls the Euclidean gradient and directional derivative u . grad f as the model. The product rule applied to v^mu e_mu gives a component term and a basis-vector term; the latter is expanded on the basis to define connection coefficients (Christoffel symbols) Gamma^lambda_{alpha mu}, which say how neighbouring local coordinate systems are connected. Example 7.4 reads off the polar-coordinate Gammas from known derivatives of e_r and e_theta, showing that flat space can have non-zero Gamma. The Gammas used in the book are symmetric in their lower indices (torsion free), and Example 7.5 quotes their transformation law, whose second-derivative term shows they are not tensor components.
concepts: Christoffel symbols of plane polar coordinates
key_moves: Word equation: covariant derivative = change in vector minus change due to coordinate system (7.1)
Directional derivative in Euclidean space as template (7.2-7.4)
Product rule on v^mu e_mu isolates the basis-vector term (7.5)
Define Gamma by expanding de_mu/dx^alpha on the basis (7.6)
Polar coordinates: read off Gamma^theta_{r theta} = Gamma^theta_{theta r} = 1/r and Gamma^r_{theta theta} = -r from derivatives of basis vectors (7.7-7.8)
Non-zero Gamma in flat space means Gamma alone cannot diagnose curvature
Symmetry Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} = Gamma^mu_{beta alpha} assumed throughout (7.9)
Inhomogeneous term in the transformation law spoils tensor behaviour (7.10-7.11)

sections.title: The covariant derivative
sections.summary: Substitutes the definition of Gamma into the product-rule expression and relabels dummy indices to obtain nabla_alpha v = (dv^mu/dx^alpha + Gamma^mu_{alpha lambda} v^lambda) e_mu, a vector for each alpha. Margin notes clarify that components of the derivative differ from derivatives of components, write nabla acting on components and on basis vectors separately, and introduce comma (partial) and semicolon (covariant) notation. In flat Cartesian coordinates all Gammas vanish and the covariant derivative reduces to partial derivatives (Example 7.6). A connection operator nabla is introduced so that e_alpha . nabla = nabla_alpha; acting on scalars it is the partial derivative, and replacing e_alpha by any u gives directional derivatives nabla_u f and nabla_u v = u^alpha nabla_alpha v. Parallel transport along u is the statement nabla_u v = 0, which in components says the change of components is entirely due to the Gamma term (Example 7.7).
concepts: components of a derivative versus derivatives of components
key_moves: Insert (7.6) into (7.5) and relabel dummies to factor out e_mu (7.12-7.13)
Rename the result nabla_alpha v and note its (1,0) character for fixed alpha (7.18)
Distinguish (nabla_alpha v)^mu from dv^mu/dx^alpha; nabla_alpha e_mu = Gamma^lambda_{alpha mu} e_lambda (7.15-7.17)
Flat Cartesian check: Gamma = 0 recovers partial derivatives (7.19)
Define nabla via e_alpha . nabla = nabla_alpha, act on scalars, extend linearly to any direction u (7.20-7.23)
Parallel transport: nabla_u v = 0 (7.24), components obey u^alpha(dv^mu/dx^alpha + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} v^beta) = 0 (7.25)
Interpretation: component change equals coordinate-induced change (7.26-7.27)

sections.title: Parametrized paths
sections.summary: Recasts the covariant derivative for curves such as world lines. A curve is x(lambda) with lambda increasing monotonically between endpoints (Fig. 7.4); Example 7.8 parametrizes a line, a parabola and a circle. If lambda is an allowed parameter, any linear re-labelling lambda = alpha eta + beta is equally good; the book calls such parametrizations affine. For a vector field v(x), the rate of change along the curve is written Dv/dlambda and equals nabla_u v with the tangent u = (dx^mu/dlambda) e_mu (Fig. 7.5); choosing lambda = tau for massive particles makes u the velocity with u.u = -1. Example 7.9 gives the limit recipe: transport v from lambda_0 + epsilon back to lambda_0, subtract v(lambda_0), divide by epsilon (Fig. 7.6). Example 7.10 checks that in flat Cartesian coordinates the components of DA/dlambda are just dA^alpha/dlambda by the chain rule.
concepts: limit definition of the covariant derivative via parallel transport
key_moves: Curve as x(lambda) with a monotonic parameter marking progress (Fig. 7.4, Example 7.8)
Affine reparametrization: linear relation between parameters
Define Dv/dlambda for a vector field along a curve (7.28)
Tangent vector u = (dx^mu/dlambda) e_mu supplies the direction (7.29), so Dv/dlambda = nabla_u v (7.30)
Proper time as parameter gives four-velocity with u.u = -1
Operational definition: parallel transport back, subtract, divide, take limit (7.31, Fig. 7.6)
Flat-space check via chain rule: (DA/dlambda)^alpha = dA^alpha/dlambda (7.32)

sections.title: Enter the metric
sections.summary: Asks whether the covariant derivative could have been built differently and answers that the metric removes the freedom: the connection must be compatible, nabla_alpha g = 0, i.e. g_{mu nu;alpha} = 0. Margin notes quote the covariant derivatives of (0,2) and (2,0) tensors and reinterpret affine parameters in terms of vector lengths under transport. Example 7.11 argues that if a parallel vector A keeps its length g_{mu nu}A^mu A^nu, the product rule forces g_{mu nu;alpha} = 0. Because g_{mu nu} = e_mu . e_nu and Gamma describes how e_mu change, Gamma should be a combination of first derivatives of the metric, summarized by the boxed rule dg -> Gamma, with the explicit formula (7.37) promised for Chapter 9.
concepts: preservation of vector length under parallel transport
key_moves: The metric, not free choice, fixes the connection: impose nabla g = 0 (7.33)
Quote tensor covariant derivatives: minus Gamma per lower index, plus Gamma per upper index (7.34-7.35)
Without compatibility, lengths would drift under parallel transport, which is physically unacceptable
Product rule on g(A,A) with A^mu_{;alpha} = 0 isolates g_{mu nu;alpha} (7.36)
g_{mu nu} = e_mu . e_nu plus Gamma from de_mu/dx^alpha suggests Gamma is built from first derivatives of g (7.38, 7.37)

sections.title: Chapter summary
sections.summary: Three bullet points: parallel transport compares vectors at different points by keeping components fixed in local frames; the covariant derivative nabla_u v measures genuine change of vector fields and has the component form of eqn 7.39; the proper-time tangent to a massive particle's world line is a timelike velocity with u.u = -1.
key_moves: Restates eqn 7.23 as 7.39
Omits metric compatibility from the summary even though §7.5 introduced it

concepts.name: manifold
concepts.definition: A space that can be covered by overlapping local coordinate patches, each looking like ordinary R^n, which join smoothly where they overlap; spacetime is modelled as a 4-dimensional manifold.
concepts.how_introduced: Through covering the curved Earth with many small rectangular street maps that blend into one another; a margin note adds the image of a smooth rubber surface such as a sphere or torus.
concepts.notes: Full treatment promised in Part V and Appendix C. The rubber-sheet note speaks of not being punctured, which is loose: a plane with a point removed is still a manifold.

concepts.name: differential geometry
concepts.definition: The mathematical study of smooth spaces (manifolds) using calculus: tangent vectors, connections, curvature and related structures.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in passing in Example 7.1 as the subject of Part V.

concepts.name: local flatness
concepts.definition: Over a sufficiently small region around any point, a smooth spacetime can be described by coordinates in which it looks like Minkowski spacetime; curvature only becomes apparent over larger separations.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted as a consequence of smoothness in Example 7.1, continuing the street-map analogy.
concepts.notes: Precisely, the metric can be made Minkowski with vanishing first derivatives at a point; second derivatives (curvature) cannot be removed. Developed in GA ch6 §6.4 and ch10.

concepts.name: intrinsic (insider) viewpoint on geometry
concepts.definition: Geometry of a space should be describable using only measurements made within the space itself, without reference to any higher-dimensional space in which it might be embedded; this is the only viewpoint available for spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Ants confined to a football and humans confined to the Earth's surface are forbidden to float above it; this rules out chord vectors and motivates tangent vectors and insider parallelism.
concepts.notes: Part V (Chapter 30, Classical curvature) returns to curvature of surfaces judged from inside versus from an embedding; Appendix D treats embedding.

concepts.name: tangent vector to a curve
concepts.definition: For a curve x^mu(lambda), the vector u = (dx^mu/dlambda) e_mu at each point, which lies in the tangent space at that point and gives the direction and rate of progress along the curve.
concepts.how_introduced: First qualitatively in §7.1 as the replacement for chord vectors on a curved surface; later in §7.4 as the direction needed to take a covariant derivative along a curve (Fig. 7.5).
concepts.notes: Margin note 14 stresses that it is not written dx/dlambda because the position vector x does not transform properly in general coordinates.

concepts.name: parallelism in curved space
concepts.definition: Two vectors at different points of a curved space are called parallel (relative to a chosen path) when one is obtained from the other by parallel transport; for insiders this means they have the same components in local frames that have themselves been carried along the path.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from the tangent of a non-turning path (great circle) and generalized by transporting the insiders' local axes; contrasted with vectors that are parallel in the embedding space but not tangent to the sphere (Fig. 7.2).
concepts.notes: The book does not emphasize here that the outcome depends on the path taken; that path dependence becomes the curvature test in Chapter 11.

concepts.name: parallel transport
concepts.definition: Moving a vector along a curve so that it undergoes no intrinsic change, i.e. its covariant derivative along the curve's tangent vanishes, nabla_u v = 0; all apparent change in its components is then due to the changing coordinate basis.
concepts.how_introduced: Pictorially in §7.1 (great circles on a sphere, Figs 7.1 and 7.3), then as the equation nabla_u v = 0 in §7.3, then as the ingredient of the limit definition of D/dlambda in §7.4 (Fig. 7.6).
concepts.notes: Along a curve the condition is best written dv^mu/dlambda + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} u^alpha v^beta = 0; the book's eqn 7.26, which drops u^alpha, only holds for a field that is parallel in every direction.

concepts.name: position-dependent basis vectors
concepts.definition: In curvilinear coordinates (and in any coordinates on a curved space) the coordinate basis vectors e_mu differ from point to point, so differentiating a vector v = v^mu e_mu requires differentiating the basis as well as the components.
concepts.how_introduced: Through the product rule in eqn 7.5 and the explicit plane polar example, where e_r = cos theta e_x + sin theta e_y and e_theta = -r sin theta e_x + r cos theta e_y (margin note 6).

concepts.name: directional derivative
concepts.definition: The rate of change of a field along a given vector u; for a scalar f in Euclidean space it is u . grad f = u^i df/dx^i, roughly the value of f at the tip of u minus its value at the base for small u.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 7.3 recalls it from vector calculus as the template that the covariant derivative generalizes; later nabla_u f = u^alpha df/dx^alpha (7.21).
formulas: \vec{u}\cdot\vec{\nabla} f = u^x \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + u^y \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} + u^z \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}
concepts.notes: The tip-minus-base reading (7.4) is only first-order accurate and needs division by the length of u to be a rate.

concepts.name: gradient
concepts.definition: For a scalar field in Euclidean 3-space, the vector of partial derivatives, grad f = (df/dx) e_x + (df/dy) e_y + (df/dz) e_z, which points normal to surfaces of constant f.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in Example 7.3 as background for the directional derivative.
formulas: \vec{\nabla} f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\vec{e}_x + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\vec{e}_y + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\vec{e}_z
concepts.notes: Chapter 31 revisits the gradient as a 1-form rather than a vector.

concepts.name: covariant derivative
concepts.definition: A derivative of vector (and tensor) fields that measures only the genuine change of the field, removing the part caused by position-dependent basis vectors; in coordinates (nabla_alpha v)^mu = dv^mu/dx^alpha + Gamma^mu_{alpha lambda} v^lambda, and the result transforms as a tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in words (eqn 7.1) as change of vector minus change due to coordinates, then derived by applying the product rule to v^mu e_mu and substituting the connection coefficients (7.12-7.18).
concepts.notes: For fixed alpha, nabla_alpha v is a vector; with alpha left free, nabla v is a (1,1) tensor (used in Exercise 7.3d).

concepts.name: connection coefficients
concepts.definition: Functions Gamma^lambda_{alpha mu}(x) defined by expanding the derivative of a basis vector on the basis, de_mu/dx^alpha = Gamma^lambda_{alpha mu} e_lambda; they tell how local frames at neighbouring points are related and supply the correction term in covariant derivatives.
concepts.how_introduced: Needed to express the awkward basis-vector term in the product rule (7.5); read as the rate at which e_mu turns toward e_lambda when moving along e_alpha (margin note 8); computed by brute force for polar coordinates.
concepts.notes: The book prefers 'connection coefficients' to 'Christoffel symbols'. In a genuinely curved space with no embedding, eqn 7.6 is really a definition of how to compare nearby tangent spaces, not something derivable; this subtlety is left to Part V.

concepts.name: Christoffel symbols of plane polar coordinates
concepts.definition: For the flat plane in (r, theta) coordinates the only non-zero connection coefficients are Gamma^theta_{r theta} = Gamma^theta_{theta r} = 1/r and Gamma^r_{theta theta} = -r.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 7.4 differentiates the polar basis vectors expressed on the Cartesian basis and reads off coefficients using eqn 7.6.
concepts.notes: Reused in Exercise 7.3(c), which asks for covariant derivatives in polar coordinates 'using the connection coefficients given in the chapter'. Chapter 9 gives a faster way to obtain the same values from the metric.

concepts.name: non-zero connection coefficients do not imply curvature
concepts.definition: Connection coefficients can be non-zero purely because of curvilinear coordinates on a flat space, so their presence cannot decide whether a space is curved; a curvature test needs a combination of Gamma and its derivatives (the Riemann tensor).
concepts.how_introduced: Drawn as the moral of Example 7.4 with a forward pointer to Chapter 11.
prerequisites: Christoffel symbols of plane polar coordinates

concepts.name: torsion-free (symmetric) connection
concepts.definition: A connection whose coefficients in a coordinate basis are symmetric in the two lower indices, Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} = Gamma^mu_{beta alpha}; equivalently its torsion tensor vanishes.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a property holding in all the coordinate frames used in the book (eqn 7.9), and used to excuse the choice of lower-index ordering.
concepts.notes: True in coordinate bases for the Levi-Civita connection; in non-coordinate (e.g. orthonormal) bases connection coefficients need not be symmetric, which matters in Chapter 10 and Cartan's method (Chapter 36).

concepts.name: non-tensorial transformation of connection coefficients
concepts.definition: Under a change of coordinates the connection coefficients pick up an extra term involving second derivatives of the old coordinates with respect to the new ones, so they do not transform as tensor components and can be made zero at a point by a suitable coordinate choice.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 7.5 contrasts the tensor transformation law (7.10) with the quoted law for Gamma (7.11), deferring the proof to Part V.
formulas: \Gamma^{\alpha'}{}_{\gamma'\beta'} = \frac{\partial x^{\alpha'}}{\partial x^\alpha}\left(\frac{\partial^2 x^\alpha}{\partial x^{\beta'}\partial x^{\gamma'}} + \frac{\partial x^\beta}{\partial x^{\beta'}}\frac{\partial x^\gamma}{\partial x^{\gamma'}}\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\gamma\beta}\right)
concepts.notes: The book offers this as the reason for the names 'coefficients' and 'symbols'. The connection to local flatness (Gamma can be transformed away at a point) is not drawn here.

concepts.name: tensor transformation law
concepts.definition: Components of an (m,n) tensor transform with one Jacobian factor dx'/dx for each upper index and one dx/dx' for each lower index, with no additional terms.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in Example 7.5 for a (1,2) object as the standard against which Gamma fails.
formulas: T^{\alpha'}{}_{\gamma'\beta'} = \frac{\partial x^{\alpha'}}{\partial x^\alpha}\frac{\partial x^\beta}{\partial x^{\beta'}}\frac{\partial x^\gamma}{\partial x^{\gamma'}} T^\alpha{}_{\gamma\beta}

concepts.name: comma and semicolon notation
concepts.definition: Shorthand in which a comma before an index denotes a partial derivative, f_{,alpha} = df/dx^alpha, and a semicolon denotes a covariant derivative, v^mu_{;alpha} = (nabla_alpha v)^mu.
concepts.how_introduced: Shaded margin box in §7.3, with the authors' remark that compactness comes at the price of punctuation-heavy expressions.

concepts.name: components of a derivative versus derivatives of components
concepts.definition: The mu-component of the covariant derivative of v is generally not the derivative of the component v^mu, because the basis vectors also change; nabla_alpha acting on the scalar functions v^mu gives dv^mu/dx^alpha, while nabla_alpha e_mu = Gamma^lambda_{alpha mu} e_lambda supplies the rest.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 10 with eqns 7.15-7.17, reinforced in margin note 13 for D/dlambda.
concepts.notes: Eqn 7.16 treats each v^mu as a scalar function, which is a notational convention; the combination is not a tensor.

concepts.name: connection operator
concepts.definition: The operator nabla defined so that e_alpha . nabla = nabla_alpha; contracting it with any vector u gives the covariant derivative along u, nabla_u = u . nabla = u^alpha nabla_alpha.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in §7.3 to pass from derivatives along basis directions to derivatives along arbitrary vectors, by analogy with u . grad f.
concepts.notes: The dot notation u . nabla is informal; in Part V nabla v is treated as a (1,1) tensor into whose slot u is inserted.

concepts.name: covariant derivative of a scalar
concepts.definition: Acting on a scalar field, the covariant derivative is simply the partial derivative, nabla_alpha f = df/dx^alpha, because a scalar has no basis vectors to change; along a curve Df/dlambda = df/dlambda.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in eqn 7.20 as the starting point for the connection operator; restated in margin note 13.

concepts.name: directional covariant derivative
concepts.definition: The covariant derivative of v in the direction of a vector u, nabla_u v = u^alpha nabla_alpha v = u^alpha (dv^mu/dx^alpha + Gamma^mu_{alpha lambda} v^lambda) e_mu, linear in u.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by replacing the basis direction e_alpha with a general vector u in eqn 7.20 and applying the same rule to vectors (7.22-7.23); becomes the chapter summary formula 7.39.

concepts.name: parallel transport equation
concepts.definition: The component statement of parallel transport along u: u^alpha dv^mu/dx^alpha + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} u^alpha v^beta = 0, meaning the change in components is exactly compensated by the connection term.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 7.7 writes out nabla_u v = 0 in components and interprets it with a word equation (7.27).
concepts.notes: With u^alpha d/dx^alpha = d/dlambda this becomes the ODE dv^mu/dlambda = -Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} u^alpha v^beta, which is what one integrates along a curve; applied to v = u it is the geodesic equation of Chapter 8.

concepts.name: parametrized curve
concepts.definition: A curve described by coordinate functions x^mu(lambda) of a parameter lambda that increases monotonically along it from one endpoint value to the other.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 1 with Fig. 7.4 and the examples of a line, parabola and circle in R^2 (Example 7.8).

concepts.name: affine parameter
concepts.definition: A parameter along a curve that is related to a preferred parameter (arc length for spacelike curves, proper time for timelike ones, or any parameter making a geodesic's tangent parallel transported) by a linear map lambda = alpha eta + beta; for non-null curves it keeps the length of the tangent vector constant.
concepts.how_introduced: Given loosely as parameters that mark off regular intervals, with any linear rescaling lambda = alpha eta + beta also allowed; margin note 16 later ties it to lengths under parallel transport, and Exercise 7.2 contrasts arc length s on a unit circle with the non-affine t = sin s.
concepts.notes: The book's characterization is imprecise (see gaps); the sharp statement comes with the geodesic equation in Chapter 8, where only affine parameters give D u/dlambda = 0.

concepts.name: vector field
concepts.definition: An assignment of a vector (in the tangent space) to each point of a region of spacetime, v(P).
concepts.how_introduced: Described in §7.4 as a machine taking a position and returning a vector there, whose rate of change along a curve is sought.

concepts.name: covariant derivative along a curve
concepts.definition: The rate of intrinsic change of a vector field along a parametrized curve, Dv/dlambda = nabla_u v with u the tangent; in components (Dv/dlambda)^mu = dv^mu/dlambda + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} u^alpha v^beta.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by a word equation (7.28, 7.30) identifying it with nabla_u v, then pictured as a limit using parallel transport back along the curve (7.31, Fig. 7.6).
concepts.notes: The book reserves D/dlambda for an affine parameter, but the definition works for any parameter; affine parameters matter for geodesics.

concepts.name: four-velocity
concepts.definition: The tangent vector to a massive particle's world line parametrized by proper time, u = (dx^mu/dtau) e_mu, normalized so that u . u = -1 in the book's signature.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the preferred special case of the tangent vector (lambda = tau) in §7.4 and in the chapter summary.
concepts.notes: Introduced in special relativity in Part I; here it becomes the u in D/dtau used for free fall in Chapter 8.

concepts.name: limit definition of the covariant derivative via parallel transport
concepts.definition: Dv/dlambda at lambda_0 is the limit, as epsilon goes to zero, of [v(lambda_0 + epsilon) parallel transported back to lambda_0, minus v(lambda_0)] divided by epsilon; transport makes the two vectors live in the same tangent space so their difference is meaningful.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 7.9 presents it as a four-step recipe modelled on [f(x + dx) - f(x)]/dx and illustrates it with Fig. 7.6.
concepts.notes: Revisited pictorially in Chapter 34 (covariant derivative in pictures).

concepts.name: metric compatibility of the connection
concepts.definition: The requirement that the covariant derivative of the metric tensor vanishes, nabla_alpha g = 0, so that parallel transport preserves lengths and angles; together with a symmetric (torsion-free) connection it fixes Gamma uniquely in terms of the metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as the answer to 'could we have defined the derivative differently?'; justified in Example 7.11 by demanding that a parallel vector keep its length.
concepts.notes: The book implies the metric alone forces the connection; uniqueness also needs the symmetry (7.9). Exercise 7.4 verifies compatibility directly from eqn 7.37.

concepts.name: preservation of vector length under parallel transport
concepts.definition: For a metric-compatible connection, the inner product g(A, B) of two vectors parallel transported along the same curve is constant, so lengths and angles are unchanged by transport.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the physical reason compatibility must hold (a world in which rulers change length on being moved would be unphysical), and used as the premise of Example 7.11.

concepts.name: Leibniz rule for covariant derivatives
concepts.definition: The covariant derivative of a tensor product or contraction of tensors obeys the ordinary product rule: differentiate each factor in turn with the others held fixed and add the results; for the squared length of a vector this yields one term containing the derivative of the metric and two containing the derivative of the vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Assumed in Example 7.11 with a margin note deferring justification to Part V; also used implicitly in eqn 7.5.
